title: Granular prefetch safety and eviction commit protocol for KV cache under continuous batching
creator: Priya Kothari
description:
Summary:
We need a provably-safe, low-latency eviction/commit protocol for our KV cache that supports: continuous batching, aggressive prefetching, prefix-aware retention, and GPU memory slab sharing. The goal is to introduce a lightweight commit/abort contract for prefetched entries (and their associated slices) so that evictions driven by LRU/TTL/space-pressure do not violate correctness of in-flight token generation or cause silent model regressions.

Background & problem statement:
- Continuous batching increases concurrency: many requests share a KV cache and may prefetch contiguous prefix blocks for future decode steps.
- Prefetching improves throughput but complicates eviction: prefetched slices can be referenced by in-flight decodes, speculative beams, or later requests that become active as batches evolve.
- GPU memory optimization relies on slab/arena allocation and shared slices to reduce fragmentation. Evicting a slice must reclaim memory without violating guarantees for other users or interrupting ongoing inference.
- Existing heuristics (LRU/TTL/prefix-affinity) do not encode safety for prefetched slices or provide atomic commit semantics when we need to evict partially-consumed prefixes.

Goals & success criteria:
- Define a commit/lease protocol for KV slices that: (1) prevents evictions of slices still referenced by in-flight decodes, (2) allows safe preemption when necessary with defined fallback, and (3) supports fast reclamation for non-referenced memory.
- Provide formal invariants and an implementable algorithm compatible with our runtime scheduler and batching system.
- Ensure overhead < 3% p99 latency for typical small- to mid-size workloads and no measurable throughput regression for large batched workloads.
- Rollout path with canary, monitoring, and automatic fallback to previous eviction policy.

Proposed design (high level):
1) Slice lease metadata: every KV slice is associated with a small lease record: {lease_id, holder_count, epoch_version, prefix_keys, ttl_hint}. The runtime increments holder_count when a decode or batch references a slice; prefetch operations create a provisional lease (holder_count=0, provisional=true).
2) Two-phase commit for prefetch: prefetch creates provisional slices. When a request actually uses the slice, it issues an 'acquire' which flips provisional->committed and increments holder_count. If a provisional slice expires without acquisition before its ttl_hint, a background scavenger can reclaim it cheaply.
3) Eviction decision: eviction candidates are scored by a combined policy: score = alpha*LRU_rank + beta*ttl_expiry + gamma*prefix_affinity_penalty + delta*provisional_penalty. Candidates with holder_count>0 are excluded. For tied candidates or under emergency pressure, we allow 'preemptive abort' where provisional slices can be evicted and any dependent speculative work is failed-over to the fallback model variant.
4) Atomic reclamation: to reclaim GPU memory we use a small per-slice fence token updated via the allocator's epoch. Reclamation proceeds only when holder_count==0 AND epoch_version <= current_epoch. This guarantees no in-flight kernel will touch freed memory.
5) Fast path for small prefixes: for prefixes smaller than a configurable threshold we permit a coalesced eviction that rewrites adjacent slices into a compacted slice to reduce per-slice overhead and fragmentation with minimal pause.

Correctness invariants (to be proven/tested):
- Safety invariant: No slice that is referenced by an in-flight decode/kernel will be freed until holder_count transitions to zero and reclamation fence has advanced past the epoch when the last holder released.
- Prefix-consistency invariant: If a decode depends on a contiguous prefix, either all constituent slices of that prefix remain available for the duration of the decode or the decode is signaled to fallback early (deterministic failure path).
- Determinism invariant: Under identical request sequences and scheduling events, eviction decisions may vary for optimization but must not change functional outputs unless an approved fallback path is executed and recorded.

Proof sketch & reasoning:
- Model holder_count and epochs as monotonically-updated counters. Show that any kernel that holds a reference must increment holder_count before using the slice and decrement after. The allocator uses epochs to order reclamation: reclamation of slice S at epoch E only proceeds if last_release_epoch(S) < E. By coupling these counters, we can show absence of use-after-free.

Compatibility with continuous batching and prefetching:
- Batching scheduler must acquire provisional slices lazily: when the scheduler decides to pin the prefix for the batch, it should perform acquire to convert provisional to committed atomically before kernel dispatch.
- For beams/speculation, we treat speculative users as normal holders; if speculation is aborted we decrement holder_count accordingly.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- Prototype metadata and allocator extension (C++ low-level) + unit tests for holder_count and epoch fences (2w).
- Integrate with continuous batching scheduler and prefetch path, instrumenting acquire/release hooks (2w).
- Simulation harness: fuzz scheduling and eviction under heavy concurrency to find races and behavior (2w).
- E2E canary on canary infra with gated fallback to previous eviction policy and telemetry (2w).

Observability & rollouts:
- New metrics: slice_leases_total, provisional_slices, holder_count_histogram, reclamation_wait_ms, eviction_rejects_due_to_holder_count, preemptive_evictions.
- Dashboards: per-model and per-GPU memory pressure heatmap; alert on preemptive_evictions>0.1% of total evictions.
- Canary rollout sequence: 5% traffic (low-variance), 20% (multi-tenant), 100% with 24h guardrail. Auto-disable if p99 latency regresses >5% or preemptive_evictions spike above threshold.

Testing strategy:
- Unit: holder_count invariants, provisional timeouts, epoch fencing.
- Integration: simulated batching and prefetch race tests under stress (fuzz harness).
- Load: p99 latency/throughput comparison with legacy policy across three representative workloads and two GPU types.
- Chaos: forced kernel delays and abrupt worker restarts to validate reclamation fence soundness.

Documentation & follow-ups:
- Confluence design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/RUNTIME/pages/GRANULAR+PREFETCH+SAFETY (placeholder)
- Implementation PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/XXXX
- Runbook for fallback and incident response: link to runbook (placeholder)

Risks & open questions:
- Overhead of holder_count updates for extreme micro-batched workloads (1-2 token per request rate): need microbenchmarks to quantify counter update cost.
- TTL tuning for provisionals: conservative ttl may waste memory, aggressive ttl may evict useful prefetched slices.
- Behavior when multiple prefixes overlap and share slices: need canonical ownership model to avoid thrashing.

Next actions:
